sections.title: What the Trial Asks For
sections.body:
The Trial is **one unseen problem set of eight problems, ninety marks, ninety minutes** - one mark a minute, which is the only pacing rule you need. Nothing here is new material: every problem is assembled from the nine floors you have already cleared, but no problem announces which floor it came from.

Marks are for **argument**, not for the final number. A correct answer with no justification scores a fraction of a fully reasoned one, and a wrong final number reached by a clearly correct method keeps most of its marks - so write the method down even when the arithmetic collapses.

Write every answer as prose plus symbols: name the technique you are using, state what you assume, and end with the claim you set out to prove. If a problem has a numeric answer, put it on its own line so the self-check list at the bottom of the paper can confirm it.
sections.code:
THE TRIAL - 8 problems, 90 marks, 90 minutes

  #  topic                                 marks   target time
  1  sets, inclusion-exclusion                10       10 min
  2  propositional logic, truth tables         8        8 min
  3  proof technique: contraposition          12       12 min
     and contradiction
  4  induction on a summation formula         12       12 min
  5  number theory: gcd, inverses, powers     12       12 min
  6  relations and equivalence classes        10       10 min
  7  graphs: degrees and colouring            10       10 min
  8  counting and probability                 16       16 min
                                            -----      ------
                                               90       90 min

MARKING, per problem
  ~60%  a correct and complete argument
  ~25%  the right technique, named and set up
  ~15%  the final answer, stated explicitly

So: a named technique + a wrong number  >  a right number + silence.

annotations.text: One mark per minute. If a 10-mark problem has eaten 20 minutes, leave it and come back - the marks are not there any more.
The three-line marking split is why an abandoned problem should still carry a sentence naming the technique you would have used.

checkpoint.prompt: Put the five parts of a written induction proof into the order a marker expects to read them.
fragments: State the proposition $P(n)$ precisely, and say which $n$ it ranges over.
Base case: verify $P(1)$ by direct computation.
Inductive hypothesis: assume $P(k)$ holds for an arbitrary fixed $k \ge 1$.
Inductive step: derive $P(k+1)$, marking the line where the hypothesis is used.
Conclude: by the principle of induction, $P(n)$ holds for all $n \ge 1$.
checkpoint.explain: The order is not decoration - it is what makes the argument checkable. The hypothesis has to be stated before the step that consumes it, or a reader cannot tell whether you assumed $P(k)$ or quietly assumed $P(k+1)$, which is the commonest way an induction proof silently begs the question.

sections.title: Choosing the Shape of the Argument
sections.body:
Most lost marks in a timed paper are not arithmetic - they are three minutes spent pushing a **direct proof** at a claim whose hypothesis is useless. The shape of the claim tells you the shape of the proof, and there are only five shapes worth reaching for.

A universal claim over $\mathbb{N}$ invites **induction**. An implication whose conclusion is easier to negate than its hypothesis is to use invites **contraposition**, since $P \Rightarrow Q$ and $\neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P$ are the same statement. A claim that no object exists invites **contradiction**: assume one does and derive an impossibility.

Two more: a claim of the form $\forall x,\ P(x)$ is destroyed by a single **counterexample**, and a claim that two finite sets have equal size is often cleanest as a **bijection**. Pick the shape in the first thirty seconds, write its name down, and the rest of the problem becomes bookkeeping.
sections.code:
PICKING THE SHAPE - read the claim, not the topic

  claim looks like                          reach for
  ----------------------------------------  --------------------
  for all n >= 1, P(n)                      induction
  P => Q, and ~Q is the easy end to hold    contraposition
  no x has property P / x is irrational     contradiction
  for all x, P(x)   (and you doubt it)      one counterexample
  |A| = |B|, both finite                    a bijection A -> B

WORKED: for every integer n, if n^2 is even then n is even.

  direct:          n^2 = 2k  =>  n = sqrt(2k)   ... stuck, no integers here
  contrapositive:  if n is odd then n^2 is odd
                   n = 2m + 1
                   n^2 = 4m^2 + 4m + 1 = 2(2m^2 + 2m) + 1   -> odd
                   done, and it took three lines

The two statements are logically identical, so proving the second
proves the first. Nothing was lost by turning the claim around.

annotations.text: The direct attempt fails for a structural reason: an even square hands you a square root, and square roots leave the integers. That is the signal to turn the claim around.
Odd is a constructive hypothesis - it hands you the witness $m$ immediately. That is almost always why the contrapositive is the easier direction.

checkpoint.prompt: Complete the technique-selection table. One word per blank, drawn from: induction, contrapositive, contradiction, counterexample.
checkpoint.template:
for all $n \ge 1$, $P(n)$   ->   prove by ___
$P \Rightarrow Q$, with $\neg Q$ the easier end to grab   ->   prove the ___
no object with the stated property exists   ->   prove by ___
the claim $\forall x,\ P(x)$ is false   ->   exhibit one ___
checkpoint.explain: Contraposition and contradiction get confused under time pressure because both open by negating something. The difference is what gets negated: contraposition negates only the conclusion and stays a direct argument, while contradiction negates the whole claim and must end at an explicit impossibility. If your contradiction never reaches an absurdity, it was a contrapositive all along.

sections.title: Checking an Answer You Cannot Run
sections.body:
Nothing executes in this dungeon, so **verification is a step you write, not a button you press**. Every closed form you derive can be tested against a small case in under a minute, and a formula that fails at $n = 1$ has just saved you the twelve marks you were about to lose.

The cheap checks are worth memorising. A probability must land in $[0, 1]$; a count must be a non-negative integer; a residue modulo $m$ must lie in $\{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$; an inclusion-exclusion total can never exceed $|U|$; the edge count implied by a degree sum must come out whole.

When a check fails, the fastest repair is to re-derive the smallest case by hand rather than to re-read the algebra. Budget the last five minutes of the ninety for exactly this sweep across all eight answers.
sections.code:
VERIFY A CLOSED FORM BY TESTING SMALL n

claim:  sum_{i=1..n} i * 2^i  =  (n - 1) * 2^(n+1) + 2

  n = 1   left:  1*2                       = 2
          right: (1-1) * 2^2 + 2 = 0 + 2   = 2      agree

  n = 2   left:  1*2 + 2*4                 = 10
          right: (2-1) * 2^3 + 2 = 8 + 2   = 10     agree

  n = 3   left:  1*2 + 2*4 + 3*8           = 34
          right: (3-1) * 2^4 + 2 = 32 + 2  = 34     agree

Two agreeing cases are not a proof. But one DISagreeing case is a
disproof, and it costs thirty seconds to look for.

CHEAP SANITY CHECKS
  probability in [0,1]      |  count is a non-negative integer
  residue mod m in [0,m-1]  |  |A u B u C| <= |U|
  sum of degrees is even    |  edges = (sum of degrees) / 2 is whole

annotations.text: $n = 1$ is where a mis-stated closed form fails first: an off-by-one in the exponent or the constant shows up immediately at the smallest input.
This asymmetry is the whole point. Testing cases can only refute, never confirm, so it belongs in front of the proof as a filter rather than in place of it.

checkpoint.prompt: Verify the closed form $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i \cdot 2^i = (n-1)2^{n+1} + 2$ at two small values of $n$. Give each value as a plain integer, and answer the last step with yes or no.

steps.label: the closed form at $n = 1$, that is $(1-1)2^{2} + 2$
the closed form at $n = 3$, that is $(3-1)2^{4} + 2$
has the formula survived both tests? (yes / no)

checkpoint.explain: Agreement at $n = 1$ and $n = 3$ establishes nothing about $n = 40$, since infinitely many false formulas pass any finite sample. What the check buys is asymmetric: it cannot confirm the claim, but it can kill a mis-copied one before you spend twelve marks' worth of time inducting on it.

trial.prompt:
**THE TRIAL. Eight problems, 90 marks, 90 minutes.** Work in one continuous sitting, closed book. Answer every part in the one answer box, numbered `1(a)`, `1(b)`, and so on. Marks are for the argument: name your technique, state your assumptions, and put each numeric answer on its own line. The self-check list at the foot of the paper holds the required final answers - do not read it until you have finished.

**Problem 1 - Sets and inclusion-exclusion (10 marks).** Let $U = \{1, 2, \dots, 30\}$, and inside $U$ let $A$ be the multiples of $2$, $B$ the multiples of $3$, and $C$ the multiples of $5$.

- (a) Compute $|A \cup B \cup C|$ by inclusion-exclusion, showing all seven terms.
- (b) Hence compute $|\overline{A \cup B \cup C}|$, the number of elements of $U$ divisible by none of $2$, $3$, $5$.
- (c) In one sentence, say why $|A \cap B| = 5$ is obtained by counting multiples of $6$ rather than by multiplying $|A|$ and $|B|$.

**Problem 2 - Propositional logic (8 marks).**

- (a) Prove by truth table that $(p \Rightarrow q) \land (\neg p \Rightarrow q) \equiv q$. Show all four rows.
- (b) Is $(p \Rightarrow q) \Rightarrow (q \Rightarrow p)$ a tautology? Answer yes or no, and justify with a single row of a truth table.

**Problem 3 - Proof technique (12 marks).**

- (a) Prove that for every integer $n$, if $n^2$ is even then $n$ is even. Name the technique before you use it.
- (b) Using part (a), prove that $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational. Your argument must say exactly where the assumption that the fraction is in lowest terms is contradicted.

**Problem 4 - Induction (12 marks).**

- (a) Prove by induction that for all $n \ge 1$, $$\sum_{i=1}^{n} i \cdot 2^i = (n-1)2^{n+1} + 2.$$ Mark clearly the line in which the inductive hypothesis is used.
- (b) State the value of the sum when $n = 10$.

**Problem 5 - Number theory (12 marks).**

- (a) Compute $7^{2026} \bmod 13$. Use the order of $7$ modulo $13$ rather than repeated squaring alone, and state what that order is.
- (b) Find the multiplicative inverse of $7$ modulo $13$, as the representative in $\{0, 1, \dots, 12\}$.
- (c) Solve $7x \equiv 5 \pmod{13}$ for the least non-negative $x$.
- (d) Compute $\gcd(252, 198)$ by the Euclidean algorithm, then find integers $s, t$ with $252s + 198t = \gcd(252, 198)$.

**Problem 6 - Relations (10 marks).** Define $R$ on $S = \{1, 2, \dots, 12\}$ by $a \mathbin{R} b$ if and only if $a \equiv b \pmod 4$.

- (a) Prove that $R$ is an equivalence relation, treating reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity separately.
- (b) State the number of equivalence classes and give one representative of each.
- (c) Compute $|R|$, the number of ordered pairs $(a, b) \in S \times S$ satisfying the relation, and explain the count rather than enumerating it.

**Problem 7 - Graphs (10 marks).**

- (a) A simple graph $G$ has $10$ vertices, every one of degree $3$. How many edges does $G$ have? Justify with the degree-sum identity.
- (b) Prove that in any simple graph the number of vertices of odd degree is even.
- (c) State the chromatic number of the cycle $C_5$, with one sentence for why that many colours suffice and one for why fewer do not.

**Problem 8 - Counting and probability (16 marks).**

- (a) How many bit strings of length $10$ contain exactly four $1$s? Give the binomial coefficient and its value.
- (b) How many bit strings of length $10$ contain at least eight $1$s?
- (c) Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. Given that at least one die shows a $5$, what is the probability that the two dice sum to $8$? Give an exact fraction in lowest terms and name the rule you used.
- (d) In one sentence, say why the answer to (c) differs from the unconditional probability that the sum is $8$.

**Self-check.** The tests below list the required final answer to each numeric part. They check arithmetic only - the marks live in the reasoning above them.
trial.explain:
The paper is built so that no problem can be answered by pattern-matching to a single floor. Problem 3(b) is unreachable without 3(a), which is itself a contraposition, so two proof shapes have to be nested rather than chosen between; 5(a) is hopeless by brute force and forces you to see that the order of $7$ modulo $13$ divides $12$ and then reduce the exponent $2026$ modulo that order; 6(c) is a counting question wearing a relations costume, and rewards reading four classes of three elements as $4 \cdot 3^2$ instead of enumerating $144$ pairs; 8(c) punishes the reflex answer $5/36$, because conditioning has already shrunk the sample space from $36$ outcomes to $11$. That is the real subject of the Trial: these topics were never separate, and competence is knowing which of them a problem is secretly about.

---

**Self-check.** Compare these against your own answers before
you read the discussion above again.

- Problem 1(a): |A u B u C| — **22**
- Problem 1(b): elements of 1..30 divisible by none of 2, 3, 5 — **8**
- Problem 2(b): is (p => q) => (q => p) a tautology? — **no**
- Problem 4(b): the value of the sum at n = 10 — **18434**
- Problem 5(a): 7^2026 mod 13 — **4**
- Problem 5(b): the inverse of 7 modulo 13 — **2**
- Problem 5(c): least non-negative solution of 7x = 5 (mod 13) — **10**
- Problem 5(d): gcd(252, 198) — **18**
- Problem 6(b): number of equivalence classes — **4**
- Problem 6(c): |R|, the number of ordered pairs — **36**
- Problem 7(a): edges of a 3-regular graph on 10 vertices — **15**
- Problem 7(c): chromatic number of C_5 — **3**
- Problem 8(a): bit strings of length 10 with exactly four 1s — **210**
- Problem 8(b): bit strings of length 10 with at least eight 1s — **56**
- Problem 8(c): P(sum = 8 | at least one 5), exact fraction — **2/11**
